title: Disadvantaged Business Enterprise Program and Disadvantaged Business Enterprise in Airport Concessions Program Implementation Modifications
summary:
Three notable federal actions landed today. The FAA approved a specific safety approach that certain small drones can use to fly over people, the Transportation Department overhauled how its disadvantaged business programs work by removing race and sex presumptions, and NOAA set new fishing gear rules to protect Caribbean reef fish.

For drones, the FAA said a safety method from a Canadian company, AVSS, is an acceptable way to show a small drone can safely operate over people. It isn’t the only way, but it gives manufacturers and operators a clearer path. This benefits drone makers and service providers who want to expand flights in populated areas, and it gives the public added safety assurances. Others may feel pressure to adopt new designs or testing, and companies using different methods will still need their own approvals.

The bigger change is to federal programs meant to help small, disadvantaged businesses compete for transportation contracts and airport concessions. Going forward, applicants won’t be presumed disadvantaged because of race or sex. Everyone must show, individually, that they’ve faced social and economic barriers. States will reevaluate all currently certified firms. During that transition, agencies covered by a given state program won’t set contract targets or count participation until reevaluations finish. Supporters say this brings the programs in line with court rulings, creates a single standard for everyone, and provides legal clarity for agencies and contractors. Those who may be negatively affected include firms that relied on the old presumptions and could lose certification, small businesses facing new paperwork and narrative requirements, and state certifiers who will shoulder a short-term surge in reviews. There could also be temporary slowdowns in awards while the transition plays out. DOT is taking public comments until November 3.

In the Caribbean, NOAA is banning or limiting some types of net fishing and requiring boats targeting reef fish to have a device ready to return deep-caught fish to depth so they survive release. This should help protect habitat and improve fish survival, benefiting commercial and recreational fishers over the long term and the communities that rely on healthy reefs. In the short term, some fishers will have to change gear and practices and absorb added costs.

Key dates: the drone safety acceptance and the business program changes take effect October 3, 2025. The Caribbean fishing measures start November 3, 2025, with parts taking effect April 1, 2026.
